Performance, under the hood · Puzzle 3 · 4 of 6

The late frame

The Android course showed that a frame must be ready before the screen's next refresh. Perfetto draws that limit for every frame, next to when the frame really finished. Here's how to read the two lines, and tell your app's lateness from someone else's.

Builds on: open one to see the idea this puzzle uses.

  • Puzzle 2: Slow isn't always busy

    A system trace shows each thread's state as the kernel sees it: Running on a CPU, Runnable and waiting for one, Sleeping while blocked on a lock or a reply, or in Uninterruptible Sleep waiting for disk I/O. A slow span that's mostly Running needs faster code; mostly Sleeping or Uninterruptible Sleep, it's waiting on something else; mostly Runnable, other threads have the CPUs.

Starting from zero? The blocks under this puzzle are 3 puzzles: 0 → 1 → 2. Know them already? Start here.

The problem

Users say scrolling stutters, but only sometimes. In a trace there are hundreds of frames. Which ones were late, by how much, and was it your app's fault, or the display side's?

See it

Save this diagram as a GIF

The building block

In the Android course you saw a frame's work: the main thread measures, lays out and draws, the RenderThread hands it to the GPU, and the result must be ready for the next vsync, the display's signal that it's about to show a new frame. Since Android 12, Perfetto's FrameTimeline draws that contract for each frame, as two slices under your app:

  • Expected Timeline: the window the app was given for this frame. It starts when the Choreographer callback was scheduled; its end is the frame's deadline.
  • Actual Timeline: what really happened. It starts when Choreographer#doFrame started running and ends at whichever came later: the frame being posted to SurfaceFlinger (the RenderThread hands the finished frame over), or the GPU finishing.

When Actual ends after the deadline, the frame is janky, and FrameTimeline labels whose fault it was. "App Deadline Missed" means your app ran longer than expected. Other labels blame SurfaceFlinger or the display, and "Buffer Stuffing" means your app queued frames faster than they could be shown.

Notice that the GPU counts. A frame whose main thread finished early can still be late if the GPU work was too heavy.

So the method is: find the late frames on the Actual Timeline, then zoom into that frame's main thread and RenderThread. Read their states (puzzle 2) first, then the flame chart (puzzle 1) for the Running parts.

The analogy

A train timetable next to the actual arrival board. The timetable (Expected) says when each train should arrive; the board (Actual) says when it did. A late train is easy to spot, and the board even says whether it was the driver or the station.

Check yourself

A frame's main thread finished well before the deadline, but FrameTimeline marks it late. What can explain it?

Not quite. The expected window is the app's budget; the GPU work came on top.

Not quite. The Actual Timeline ends at the later of posting and the GPU finishing.

Right. Actual ends at max(GPU, post time).

A frame is marked "App Deadline Missed". Where do you look next?

Right. The app was late: read the app's threads.

Not quite. The window comes from the display's timing; you can't stretch it.

Not quite. That label means your app took too long; SurfaceFlinger has its own labels.

What's the difference between the Expected Timeline and the Actual Timeline?

Right. Budget vs what happened.

Not quite. That's the two swapped. Re-read that part ↑

Sources

  • Perfetto: Android Jank detection with FrameTimeline ("FrameTimeline requires Android 12(S) or higher"; "Expected Timeline: Each slice represents the time given to the app for rendering the frame… The start time is the time the Choreographer callback was scheduled to run"; "Actual Timeline: These slices represent the actual time an app took to complete the frame (including GPU work) and send it to SurfaceFlinger for composition… The end time of the slices here represent max(gpu time, post time)"; "AppDeadlineMissed: The app ran longer than expected causing a jank.")
  • Android Studio: UI jank detection (the threads relevant to a janky frame: "the UI thread, RenderThread, and the GPU completion thread")

What you now know

FrameTimeline gives every frame two slices: the Expected Timeline, the window the app was given, and the Actual Timeline, from Choreographer's callback to when the frame was posted and the GPU finished. Actual past the deadline is jank; FrameTimeline says whether the app or SurfaceFlinger was late. Then read the late frame's main thread and RenderThread: states, then flame chart.
